messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Callum is a 21-year-old white European male, currently unemployed and married, who was referred for psychological assessment following what his GP described as a significant deterioration in his daily functioning. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 42, consistent with a probable PTSD diagnosis, arising from a traumatic event involving a family member approximately eight months ago.

The precipitating event occurred when Callum witnessed a severe physical assault on his father. He had arrived home unexpectedly to find his father on the kitchen floor, badly beaten, blood visible across specific parts of his body that Callum cannot now look at without his chest constricting. The image — more photograph than memory, he says, sharp and static and impossible to move past — has lodged itself in a way that ordinary recollection does not. He cannot narrate the event sequentially; when he tries to put it into words, language seems to dissolve. What remains instead are sensory fragments: the particular smell of that room, which returns without warning when he thinks of what happened, and a series of frozen images, as though someone has pressed pause on the worst frames and left them playing on a loop.

In the weeks that followed, Callum found himself unable to tolerate reminders of what he had seen. When people around him made casual comments about family — at the shops, on the street, anywhere — he felt the memory surface immediately, the smell and the images arriving together, and with them a wave of distress that he could not contain. He began avoiding television programmes and films that might depict violence or family harm, and stopped reading the news altogether. These avoidances brought short-term relief but also meant he spent increasing hours in an unstructured, stimulus-poor environment — which, paradoxically, gave the memories more room to intrude. The more he avoided, the less he had processed, and the more raw and immediate the recollections remained.

What frightened him most in those early months was the way his body refused to settle. Sudden movements by others — a flatmate reaching across a table, a stranger gesturing on the street — sent him immediately into a state of high alert, heart hammering, muscles braced. He could not sleep reliably, lying awake rehearsing threats that might not exist, and on several occasions woke mid-flashback, convinced the assault was happening again, in the present tense. He had come to believe that his body was working against him, responding to safety as though it were danger, and this belief that he could no longer trust his own physiology became one of the most destabilising features of his presentation. The sustained threat state, in turn, made him hypervigilant to anything that resembled the original context — people acting in ways he read as suspicious, any unfamiliar movement in his peripheral vision — so that ordinary social environments became minefields he felt compelled to scan constantly.

Callum is not working, and without the structure of employment, his days have become dominated by threat monitoring and avoidance. He will not remain alone in a room or building — the silence feels dangerous, the absence of another person a condition under which something terrible might happen again — and so he organises his entire day around his wife's schedule. This has placed significant strain on their marriage; she has begun to feel less like a partner and more like a safety object, and both of them are aware of this without knowing how to name it. When the distress becomes unbearable, Callum has on several occasions hurt himself physically, describing it as the only way to interrupt the overwhelming feeling — a strategy that briefly disrupts the internal alarm but leaves him afterwards with a deepened sense that he is no longer the person he was. He is certain he is no longer capable of the things that once defined him, and he cannot rely on himself to manage even ordinary situations. These appraisals — of a self that has fundamentally broken — lower his threshold for perceiving threat in the environment, so that even neutral cues now carry a charge they would not previously have held.

Callum came to seek help after his wife found evidence of the self-harm. What he most fears is that he will never recover the person he was before that afternoon in the kitchen. What he most hopes is that someone can explain why his own mind and body have become so foreign to him.
